extra.message: The Dockerfile does not specify a non-root user for running the application. By default, the container runs as root, violating the principle of least privilege.

The Dockerfile exposes both port 5000 and port 80, and docker-compose.yml also maps both ports. The application only runs on one port, creating unnecessary exposure and potential confusion about which service is accessible where.

The Docker container runs the application as the root user. If the application is compromised, an attacker gains root access within the container, increasing the risk of container escape or host compromise.

Flask is initialized without a SECRET_KEY. Flask requires a secret key for signing session cookies and other security features. Without it, Flask's session system cannot be used securely, and many Flask extensions will refuse to work.

The application uses hardcoded credentials (username='admin', password='password123') defined as module-level constants. These credentials are embedded directly in source code and visible to anyone with access to the repository.

Passwords are stored as plain TEXT in the SQLite database with no hashing whatsoever. The INSERT statement at line 15 inserts 'password1' as cleartext. The schema at line 14 defines password as TEXT, confirming no hashing mechanism exists.

User passwords are stored in plaintext in the SQLite database during initialization. Line 15 inserts 'password1' as a raw string with no hashing. Together with the SQL injection vulnerability, an attacker can dump all plaintext passwords.
Test user credentials ('user1'/'password1') are hardcoded directly in the SQL INSERT statement during database initialization. These are valid credentials that grant access to the application.
The /login POST endpoint has no rate limiting or account lockout mechanism. An attacker can perform unlimited brute-force password attempts against any user account without throttling.

The /login endpoint accepts POST requests with no CSRF token validation. Since the application uses cookie-based sessions, an attacker can craft a malicious HTML page that submits a login form on behalf of an authenticated victim, potentially changing credentials or performing actions.

The login endpoint compares passwords as plaintext in the SQL query. Combined with the plaintext storage, this means passwords are transmitted, stored, and compared without any hashing or encryption, violating basic password security practices.

User-supplied username and password from the login form are directly interpolated into a SQL query using an f-string, allowing SQL injection. An attacker can bypass authentication or extract arbitrary data from the database.

After successful authentication (line 36 check passes), the login handler sets the session cookie but never regenerates the session ID. The cookie value is set to the plain username with no randomization, making it predictable and fixable.

The session cookie is set without the 'HttpOnly' flag, allowing client-side JavaScript to access the cookie via document.cookie. Combined with the XSS vulnerabilities in the same application, this enables cookie theft.

After successful login, the session cookie is set to the raw username string (e.g., 'admin') rather than a cryptographically random session token. There is no session ID, no expiry, no signature, and no HttpOnly/Secure flags.

The session cookie value is set to the literal username with no randomness, entropy, or cryptographic signing. An attacker can trivially forge session cookies by guessing usernames ('admin', 'user1', etc.) to impersonate any user.

The session cookie is set with only the username as the value and without HttpOnly, Secure, or SameSite flags. This makes the cookie accessible to JavaScript (allowing XSS-based cookie theft), transmitted over unencrypted HTTP, and vulnerable to CSRF.

The /dashboard endpoint does not verify that the user has authenticated via the login process. It reads any value from the 'session' cookie and renders the page without validating the session against the server-side database.

The /dashboard route has NO authentication or authorization check. Any unauthenticated user can access the dashboard page simply by visiting /dashboard. The only identification is reading the 'session' cookie with a fallback to 'guest' — no verification that the cookie value represents a valid authenticated user.

The /dashboard endpoint makes a security-relevant decision — identifying the current user — based entirely on the value of the 'session' cookie, which is set and controlled by the client. An attacker can impersonate any user simply by changing the cookie value to another username. There is no server-side session validation, signature, or integrity check.

The dashboard endpoint renders the 'session' cookie value (which is the username from login) into an HTML response via an f-string without escaping. An attacker who can set a victim's cookie value (e.g., via another XSS or by tricking login with a malicious username) can execute arbitrary JavaScript.

The search function renders user-supplied input from the 'q' query parameter directly into an HTML response via an f-string without any escaping. An attacker can craft a URL with malicious JavaScript in the q parameter and when a victim clicks it, the script executes in their browser.

The Flask app runs on port 80 (privileged port) and the Dockerfile has no USER directive, so the process runs as root. Running as root increases the blast radius of any vulnerability — code execution leads to full container compromise.

The Flask application is configured to run on host='0.0.0.0' (all interfaces) and port 80. Binding to all interfaces exposes the application on all network interfaces of the host. Running on port 80 (privileged port) also requires root privileges, increasing the attack surface if the container is compromised.
Both port 5000 and port 80 are exposed in the docker-compose configuration, increasing the attack surface. Only one port is needed for the application.

Both port 5000 and port 80 are exposed in the docker-compose configuration, but the application only listens on port 80 (line 57 of app.py). Port 5000 mapping is unnecessary and increases the attack surface.

The docker-compose.yml mounts the host's ./app directory to /app in the container. This allows host-side modifications to application code to take effect immediately inside the container. In production, this bypasses image integrity guarantees and could allow code injection if an attacker gains any write access to the host filesystem.
